young.html: George Orwell was an English writer who cared about fairness, truth and plain words. Animal Farm looks like a children's fable, but it is really a story about how a fight for freedom can go wrong.

On Manor Farm, the animals are tired of working hard for a careless farmer who keeps everything for himself. They rise up, chase him away, and run the farm together. They paint rules on the barn wall, the most important being that all animals are equal. At first things go well. But the clever pigs slowly take charge. They move into the farmhouse, change the rules a little at a time, and use fierce dogs to scare anyone who complains. In the end, the other animals can't tell the pigs from the people they drove out.

young.html: Rules for a fair game. As a family, write five rules for a game or for chores that everyone agrees are fair. Post them. A week later, read them together: did anyone "bend" a rule? Talk about why it matters that rules stay the same for everyone, and that everyone can read them.

full.html: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950), born in India, educated at Eton, and a colonial policeman in Burma before he became a writer. He described poverty in England and France, and fought for the Republican side in the Spanish Civil War, where he saw a faction backed by the Soviet Union turn on its own allies. A lifelong democratic socialist, he came to oppose the Soviet system under Stalin. Animal Farm, finished in 1944, was turned down by several publishers, partly because Britain and the Soviet Union were wartime allies; it appeared in August 1945. His last novel was Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949).
About quotations: Animal Farm was first published in 1945 and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words, including the rules in the visual.

Old Major, a respected boar, tells the animals of his dream of a world without human masters. After his death, the animals rebel, drive out the drunken farmer Mr. Jones, rename the place Animal Farm and paint their rules on the barn. Two young pigs lead: Snowball, an inventive speaker who plans a windmill, and Napoleon, quiet and scheming, who secretly raises a litter of puppies. When the dogs are grown, Napoleon uses them to chase Snowball off the farm and blames him for every later misfortune. A pig called Squealer, a gifted talker, explains away each new privilege the pigs take, and the rules on the wall are quietly altered. The loyal cart-horse Boxer works himself to exhaustion trusting the leaders, and when he collapses the pigs sell him to a slaughterer while telling the others he died in a hospital. At the end, the pigs walk on two legs, wear clothes and entertain the neighboring farmers, and the animals outside the window can no longer tell pig from man.

full.html: Orwell said plainly that the book is an allegory of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and what followed. Most readers match the characters this way:

head: In the fable
In history (as Orwell meant it)
rows: the Tsar and the old regime
full.cap: A common reading; Orwell kept some details loose so the story would apply more widely.

full.html: Orwell's warning reaches beyond one country. Power without checks corrupts those who hold it; a free people needs memory, honest records and plain language, because whoever controls the words can rewrite the rules.

Orwell did not argue that the farm should go back to Mr. Jones. The fable's target is the betrayal of a revolution's ideals by a new ruling group. Readers of many political views have claimed it; its lesson about language and power is shared widely.
Reading it as only an animal story, or only as history. It is both: a fable simple enough for children and a precise political satire.

items: Aesop's fables used animals to teach lessons, and Swift's Gulliver's Travels, earlier on this ladder, used imaginary lands for satire.
Plato's Republic asked who should rule and how rulers can be kept from serving themselves.
Marx and Engels, earlier on this ladder, wrote the ideas Old Major's dream echoes; Orwell attacks what was done in their name, not the wish for fairness.
Thucydides described how, in civil strife, words change their meanings; Orwell's Squealer shows the same.
Why do the other animals let the pigs change the rules?
What makes power safe or dangerous in the hands of a few?
Why does Orwell care so much about written rules and plain words?
What could the animals have done to keep their farm fair?

questions: Why did the animals rebel in the first place?
How did the pigs change the rules without the other animals noticing?
Boxer always trusted the leaders. Is trust always good? When should we ask questions?
Why is it important that everyone can read and remember the rules?
Is there a time someone changed the rules in a game you played? How did it feel?
care: Some animals are killed or sold to slaughter, told simply and without detail. A family-friendly fable with a serious political meaning.
